dimensions.name: Contract reverse-engineering & environment probing

evidence.note: Agent explicitly states it will inspect the workspace and dev test client BEFORE coding because 'the hidden suite will expect the exact REST shapes that helpers.py uses' — correct orientation intent before any implementation.

Systematically reads helpers.py in full plus all 12 public test files (api, engine, spill, deps, copy_fill, sort_filter, csv, xlsx, ooxml, xlsx_oracle, validation, pivot, locale, iter, collab), pinning down endpoint shapes, cell kinds, spill anchor fields, listing envelope, and collab op/event frames — the systematic endpoint/shape mapping described in anchor 8.

Probes library availability for fastapi/openpyxl/formulas/xlcalculator/pycel/lark/numpy/scipy etc. (all False), checks for libreoffice/soffice, and verifies stdlib modules (zipfile, ElementTree) — a real capability probe that drove the decision to build self-contained on stdlib.
Reads conftest.py and run.sh to understand the harness before committing, confirming how the smoke suite boots and gates.

Runs the public smoke suite early against the live server to anchor the contract, immediately surfacing the #NAME? dispatch bug — using tests as ground truth rather than relying on the invented model.

Cross-references coverage in prose ('bounded slice covering formula/spills/pivot/locale/collab') and concludes with 'I have the contract pinned down' — but contract reading is largely a single front-loaded pass rather than repeated re-probing as subsystems surface.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent went well beyond anchor 5: it read helpers.py AND every public test file to map the full set of endpoint/request shapes, ran run.sh/conftest, probed a broad list of candidate libraries plus system tools, and anchored the contract by running the smoke suite early. That matches the systematic-mapping clause of anchor 8. It falls short of a clean 8-10 because the library-capability validation was only an availability check (no installed lib meant no LET/LAMBDA/openpyxl round-trip spikes were run — it just committed to hand-rolled stdlib), and orientation was mostly front-loaded rather than re-probed across the horizon. That places it solidly at 7, between the 5 and 8 anchors.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones

evidence.note: Explicit dependency-aware ordering in the plan: read helpers.py and all public tests to pin the contract before implementing, then verify live. This is sequencing intent, not just a flat feature list.

Enumerates the subsystem set (parsing, spills, deps, CSV/XLSX, validation, pivot, locale, iterative, goal seek, collab) and probes libraries before committing to a self-contained approach — coarse but real decomposition.
The build itself was a single 92KB big-bang monolith writing ALL subsystems at once — no walking skeleton, no incremental verified-predecessor chain. This caps the level below the higher anchors.
Verification is gated by test runs; on failure it fixed the CORE evaluator dispatch bug first and re-ran engine/spill groups before the full suite — core-first milestone gating in the fix phase.

XLSX hardening explicitly deferred until the full suite was green and isolated as its own milestone with an XLSX-subset check plus a full regression re-run — dependency-aware deferral of a harder piece.
Persistence isolated as a final milestone with a concrete acceptance check (B1 == 124 survives restart), showing explicit done-conditions per milestone in the verification arc.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent had a sensible ordered plan (contracts → build → verify → harden → persistence) with genuinely gated verification milestones each carrying an explicit check, prioritized the core engine bug before other fixes, and deferred XLSX/persistence as distinct checked milestones — clearly above a flat feature to-do list (level 3). But it did not stand up a testable core early and layer features on verified predecessors; instead it wrote the entire ~dozen-subsystem product as one big-bang monolith (step 33), then verified. That absence of an incremental walking skeleton keeps it out of the level-8 band, landing it at a solid level 5.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness checks against Excel ground truth

evidence.note: Ran the live server, checked /api/health, and ran dev_tests/run.sh repeatedly (targeted groups then full 131-test suite), treating a green smoke run as the primary correctness signal. No independent cell-by-cell value checks were built for these areas.

Proactively tightened the XLSX layer, explicitly reasoning that 'hidden tests are likely to inspect style and format round-trips more deeply' — but verified the change only by re-running the smoke suite, not by building an independent openpyxl re-read oracle.

Performed one manual restart/persistence check by hand: created a workbook, set A1=123 and B1=A1+1, restarted start.sh, and confirmed B1 still evaluated to 124. This is a single hand-verified value check, focused on persistence rather than Excel semantics.

Final summary cites only 'bash run.sh -> 131 passed' and the manual restart check as verification — no self-built oracles for error sentinels, spill/ghost semantics, iterative-calc convergence, collab seq ordering, or performance budgets.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably ran the server and the full smoke suite and fixed failures against it, and it did one manual by-hand value/round-trip check (persistence: B1=124), plus showed awareness that hidden tests probe XLSX more deeply. That places it above anchor 3 (pure green-smoke-equals-done). But it never built independent targeted oracles for the high-risk areas the level-8 anchor describes (error propagation, spill mechanics, iterative calc, openpyxl re-read fidelity, collab ordering, performance budgets) — even the proactive XLSX work was validated only by re-running the smoke suite. The single trivial manual check falls short of the 'handful of formulas plus a round-trip against Excel values' of anchor 5, landing it at 4.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a vast surface

evidence.note: Read every public test file upfront and at step 25 explicitly enumerated the in-scope subsystems, establishing a coarse coverage map used as the tracking ruler; but never enumerated the individual function families (distributions, engineering, database, financial) to track done-vs-remaining across the catalog.
On 69 failures, correctly diagnosed a single shared root cause (built-in name dispatch) rather than losing track amid many red tests — an accurate read of what was actually broken vs. done.
Ran a targeted subset to confirm the fix landed, then a full-suite run to verify green across all subsystems — updating the picture as pieces landed.

After extending the XLSX layer, deliberately re-ran the XLSX/OOXML/validation subset AND the full suite to confirm the metadata work did not regress earlier subsystems — the regression-catching behavior of the higher anchors.
Ran an explicit persistence restart check and confirmed value survived, closing a known requirement rather than assuming it; recovered from a failed detached launch by reading logs.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent maintained a roughly accurate, continuously updated done-vs-remaining picture and, notably, re-ran earlier subsystem tests after later changes to catch regressions (steps 68/70), which reaches into the level-8 territory. However, its coverage tracking was driven almost entirely by the shipped smoke suite rather than an independent, precise per-function-family map across the enormous catalog it was warned was non-exhaustive; there was no systematic audit of which of the ~150 functions or optional endpoints were verified, and no explicit thrash/over-investment detection beyond one mild note at step 58. That places it solidly between the level-5 'running checklist' anchor and the level-8 'precise coverage map with rebalancing and regression re-checks' anchor.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions

evidence.note: First full suite run failed; instead of patching each #NAME? symptom, the agent root-caused it ('the evaluator was resolving built-in function names as ordinary names before dispatching them, so nearly every call became #NAME?') and applied a narrow fix to the dispatch path in eval_call — a design-level correction, not symptom whack-a-mole.
After the fix, restarted the server and re-verified with targeted engine/spill/locale groups first, then the full suite — proper re-validation of the blast radius before moving on.
Discovered `requests` unavailable in the base env and pivoted the restart smoke check to urllib — a small, clean course-correction on a falsified environment assumption.

Detached nohup start silently failed (empty log, port unbound); investigated log then port, then re-ran in foreground to isolate the immediate failure and confirm the service itself was healthy — adaptive but the root cause of the detached failure was never fully reconciled.

Chose stdlib-only implementation after probing (no libs installed), and proactively hardened XLSX metadata anticipating deeper hidden tests — but these were upfront/anticipatory decisions, not corrections of a mid-build falsified bet, so no library swap or recompute redesign was ever forced.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent reliably treated failing checks as signals: it root-caused the evaluator dispatch bug (design-level, not symptom-local), then backed up, restarted, and re-verified targeted-then-full, and handled smaller falsifications (requests→urllib, detached-start diagnosis) cleanly — clearly above the level-5 'adjusts subsystem then re-verifies' anchor. It falls short of 8/10 because the build was smooth and self-contained: there were few high-stakes falsified assumptions to overturn (no inadequate library to swap, no perf-budget miss detected, no misread wire shape corrected), so no decisive design pivot with documented blast-radius revalidation was demonstrated.

dimensions.name: Breadth-vs-depth effort allocation under a hidden suite

evidence.note: Explicitly names the breadth of the surface ('formulas, dynamic arrays, dependency propagation, CSV/XLSX, collaboration, formats, pivots, locale, validation, iterative calc') and chooses a custom evaluator to keep wire-shape control across all of it — a deliberate breadth-oriented allocation decision.

The first implementation patch (82KB) already contains all 113 catalog functions plus every subsystem (spill, locale, CSV, conditional_format, websocket, data_validation, iterative calc, pivot, goal_seek, defined names, collab). Confirmed by diffing the implemented function set against the catalog: zero missing. Effort was proportioned for wide coverage from the outset rather than gold-plating one family.

Consciously targets depth on the load-bearing, error-prone core next — 'dependency cycles, spill arrays, fill, sort/filter, and import/export paths where most contract mismatches tend to surface' — showing where depth is judged worth it versus the long tail.

After visible suite passes, runs a deliberate hardening pass explicitly 'for hidden-suite behavior' (atomic multi-cell patches, broader error classification, and functions beyond the public corpus — added CHOOSE, COLUMN, COUNTA, MAXIFS, MINIFS, IFS, SWITCH, IFNA). This is a targeted breadth-extension aimed at the unseen suite, not the visible one.

Spot-checks specific added functions (IFNA) live rather than blanket re-verifying, but re-prioritization is mostly a single linear hardening pass rather than a continuous evidence-driven loop — the reason this lands at 8 not 10.

dimensions.reasoning: The agent made explicit, sensible allocation calls: broad coverage of the entire function catalog and all optional subsystems from the first implementation (step 32), deliberate depth on the correctness-critical core (recompute, cycles, spill, import/export at step 39), and a conscious breadth-extension beyond the visible corpus aimed at the hidden suite (step 42/46/47). This matches the level-8 anchor of deep-on-load-bearing, broad-on-the-tail to maximize expected coverage. It falls short of 10 because re-prioritization was largely front-loaded and linear rather than a continuous risk-driven loop.

rubric.task_read: This is a very long-horizon, high-complexity build: a full Excel-clone product spanning an HTTP server with restart-durable persistence, a several-hundred-function Excel-365 formula engine (LET/LAMBDA, dynamic-array spilling, iterative calc, goal seek), dirty-only topological recompute under hard performance budgets, XLSX/CSV round-trips graded cell-by-cell against a LibreOffice corpus, a WebSocket collab protocol, a browser SPA with fixed testids, and a large analyst surface (names, formats, conditional formats, pivots, locale, validation). The exact wire contract is deliberately under-specified in prose and must be reverse-engineered from an existing first-party client (/dev_tests/helpers.py); the shipped smoke suite is non-exhaustive and grading is on a much larger hidden suite. A skilled practitioner would invest heavily and continuously in orientation, sequencing, self-built verification, and course-correction — meta-work is decisive here.

dimensions.name: Contract reverse-engineering & environment probing
dimensions.description: Extracting the exact wire shapes and behavioral contract from /dev_tests/helpers.py and run.sh, and probing library capabilities (OOXML I/O, formula-eval, WebSocket) before committing to an approach.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The JSON shapes, cell kind discriminator, spill fields, and listing envelope are defined ONLY by what helpers.py calls — prose is explicitly deferential to it. Acting before reading the client means building against an invented contract that the hidden suite will reject wholesale, and library choice (does the eval lib support LET/LAMBDA/spilling? does export stay openpyxl-readable?) constrains the entire design.

anchors.0: Starts coding the server/engine without opening helpers.py; invents request/response shapes from the prose alone.
anchors.3: Skims helpers.py once, copies a couple of obvious shapes, but misses spill fields, kind discriminator nuances, or the error-name contract; never checks what libraries can actually do.
anchors.5: Reads helpers.py and run.sh to pin down the main endpoint shapes and runs the smoke suite early to anchor the contract; does a basic check that chosen libraries exist.
anchors.8: Systematically maps every endpoint/shape helpers.py exercises (patch/fill/sort/filter bodies, spill anchor fields, listing envelope, collab frames), cross-references against the prose to spot gaps the client implies, and validates library capabilities (LET/LAMBDA, dynamic arrays, openpyxl round-trip fidelity) with quick spikes before designing around them.
anchors.10: Builds a precise, documented model of the full contract from the client — including edge cases the prose leaves implicit (spill ghost semantics, locale canonicalization, validation-vs-formula-write rules) — and returns to re-probe helpers.py and library behavior whenever new subsystems surface, keeping orientation current across the whole horizon rather than front-loading it once.

dimensions.name: Subsystem sequencing & verifiable milestones
dimensions.description: Breaking a ~dozen-subsystem product into an ordered hierarchy of independently checkable milestones (health/persistence → cell model → recompute → formula catalog → features), each with an explicit done-condition.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The surface is enormous and interdependent: the formula engine underlies XLSX/collab/pivots; recompute correctness underlies everything. Without dependency-aware sequencing and milestone gates, the agent either builds features on an unverified core or thrashes across the catalog with nothing end-to-end working.

anchors.0: No structure — jumps between random functions and features; no ordering, no notion of when a piece is 'done'.
anchors.3: A flat to-do list of features with no dependency ordering and no explicit done-criteria per item.
anchors.5: A sensible ordered plan that gets a walking skeleton (health, persistence, basic cells+recompute) before layering features, with rough milestones.
anchors.8: Dependency-aware milestone hierarchy that stands up a testable core early, sequences subsystems so each builds on a verified predecessor, and attaches an explicit check to each milestone; defers hard/independent pieces (collab, XLSX, goal-seek) until their foundations hold.
anchors.10: A living milestone structure that makes the walking skeleton demonstrably pass smoke tests before expansion, is re-ordered as dependencies and risks surface, and consistently isolates each subsystem behind a concrete acceptance check — enabling sustained forward progress across the full horizon without regressions in earlier milestones.

dimensions.name: Self-built correctness checks against Excel ground truth
dimensions.description: Deliberately constructing verification beyond the shipped smoke suite — running the live server, checking formula results against known Excel semantics, and validating XLSX/collab/spill behavior — since grading is on a hidden corpus.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The smoke suite is explicitly non-exhaustive and the hidden suite grades values cell-by-cell against LibreOffice. Assuming smoke-pass equals correct guarantees silent divergence across hundreds of functions, error propagation, spill mechanics, and round-trips. Only self-designed oracles catch these before grading.

anchors.0: Never runs the server or tests; assumes code works.
anchors.3: Runs dev_tests/run.sh occasionally and treats a green smoke run as done; no independent value checks.
anchors.5: Runs the server and smoke suite, and spot-checks a handful of formulas and one round-trip by hand against expected Excel values.
anchors.8: Builds its own targeted checks for high-risk areas — error-sentinel propagation, spill/ghost semantics, iterative-calc convergence, XLSX openpyxl re-read fidelity, collab seq ordering — and verifies representative functions across families against real Excel/LibreOffice-consistent expectations rather than trusting the smoke suite.
anchors.10: Establishes a reusable verification harness that exercises subsystems cell-by-cell against ground-truth expectations, covers boundary/error cases the hidden suite is likely to probe, checks performance budgets empirically (1k chain, 100k import, 5k dependents), and re-runs it as a regression guard after each change — actively hunting for divergence rather than confirming success.

dimensions.name: Coverage tracking across a vast surface
dimensions.description: Maintaining an accurate done-vs-remaining picture across dozens of function families and subsystems, and detecting when stuck on one area or regressing others.
dimensions.why_it_matters: With hundreds of functions and many subsystems over a long horizon, it is easy to lose the plot — over-polishing one function family, forgetting whole categories (engineering, distributions, database), or silently breaking recompute while adding features. Accurate progress tracking is what keeps breadth honest.

anchors.0: No sense of what's done or left; discovers omissions only by accident.
anchors.3: Vague mental tally; loses track of which function families or endpoints remain, revisits done work or forgets categories.
anchors.5: Keeps a running checklist of subsystems/functions and updates it as pieces land, giving a roughly accurate remaining-work picture.
anchors.8: Maintains a precise coverage map (per family and per endpoint), notices when it is thrashing or over-investing in one area, and rebalances; catches regressions in earlier subsystems via re-checks.
anchors.10: Sustains a fully accurate, continuously updated picture of completion and risk across the entire surface, proactively flags stuck/circular states early and reallocates, and never lets a completed subsystem silently regress across the long build.

dimensions.name: Course-correction on falsified assumptions
dimensions.description: Revising design, library choice, or approach when reality diverges — a formula-eval library that can't do LET/LAMBDA/spilling, an export that won't re-read in openpyxl, recompute that misses the performance budget, or a misread contract.
dimensions.why_it_matters: Early bets here are high-stakes and fallible: chosen libraries may not support Excel-365 semantics, naive recompute may blow the performance budgets, and the reverse-engineered contract may be wrong in spots. Barrelling ahead on a falsified assumption wastes large amounts of the horizon and cascades failures across dependent subsystems.

anchors.0: Ignores contradicting evidence (failing tests, missing library features, perf misses) and keeps building on the broken assumption.
anchors.3: Notices failures but patches symptoms locally without reconsidering the underlying approach.
anchors.5: When a check fails or a library falls short, backs up and adjusts the approach for that subsystem, then re-verifies.
anchors.8: Treats surprising failures as signals to revisit the design — e.g. swaps or wraps an inadequate eval/OOXML library, redesigns recompute to hit perf budgets, or corrects a misread wire shape — and propagates the fix to affected subsystems.
anchors.10: Detects falsified assumptions early from its own verification, makes decisive well-scoped pivots (not flailing rewrites), documents why, and re-validates the blast radius — repeatedly steering the build back on course without losing accumulated progress.

dimensions.name: Breadth-vs-depth effort allocation under a hidden suite
dimensions.description: Strategically proportioning finite effort across an enormous catalog and many optional-looking subsystems to maximize expected hidden-suite coverage, rather than perfecting a few areas while leaving whole categories absent.
dimensions.why_it_matters: The catalog is huge and grading is on an unseen, much larger suite, so marginal return comes from breadth of correct coverage, not from gold-plating one function family. Deciding where depth is worth it (recompute core, spill, error propagation) versus where breadth suffices (long tail of functions) is a distinct allocation judgment beyond ordering milestones.

anchors.0: Sinks the whole budget into one area (e.g. perfecting a few math functions or the SPA) leaving most subsystems and function families unimplemented.
anchors.3: Implements whatever is top-of-mind with no deliberate breadth/depth tradeoff; large obvious categories left untouched with no rationale.
anchors.5: Consciously spreads effort to cover most subsystems and function families at a working level, accepting rough edges on the long tail.
anchors.8: Makes explicit, sensible allocation calls — deep on the load-bearing, correctness-critical core (recompute, spill, errors, contract fidelity) and broad on the long tail — to maximize expected coverage of an unseen suite.
anchors.10: Continuously re-prioritizes allocation from evidence (which areas are risky, which cheaply broaden coverage), demonstrably maximizing correct breadth while protecting the critical core, and avoids both over-investment in one corner and shallow coverage everywhere.
